family_history: No family history of ALS or FTD

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Concrete thinking. Superficially cooperative. MoCA 21/30: loses points executive function (trails 0/1, fluency 0/1, clock drawing partial), memory (3/5 delayed recall), and language (naming 2/3). MMSE 24/30 by comparison — the discrepancy between lower MoCA and higher MMSE reflects MoCA's greater frontal/executive sensitivity.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. Bilateral snout reflex present. Bilateral grasp reflex elicited.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone. Strength 5/5 throughout. No tremor. No rigidity. No fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric. No Babinski. Grasp reflex positive bilaterally — prominent frontal release sign.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence, mildly wide-based (possible cerebellar effect of remote alcohol use). No shuffling.
neurological_exam.additional: Wife is clearly frustrated and distressed. She states her husband has been 'a completely different person' for the past 2 years. He watches football for 18 hours a day, eating chips and ignoring family. He made two large unauthorized withdrawals from their retirement savings for undisclosed purchases. He has urinated in the backyard and twice in inappropriate household locations. He has propositioned his wife's sister. The grasp reflex is prominent bilaterally — a frontal release sign indicating advanced frontal lobe dysfunction. DIAGNOSTIC CHALLENGE: Prior alcohol use history raises Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome or alcohol-related dementia as alternative. CPAP-adherent OSA ensures sleep apnea is not contributing. However, the behavioral pattern is more consistent with bvFTD than alcohol-related dementia.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive personality change, disinhibition, and inappropriate behavior — 2 years
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T is a 61-year-old retired police sergeant with a history of remote alcohol use disorder (12 years sober, active AA member), type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and treated obstructive sleep apnea who is brought to the neurology clinic by his wife. His wife has been his primary historian, as he minimizes all reported behavioral changes and insists he is 'fine.' She describes a 2-year history of progressive personality and behavioral transformation that she initially attributed to retirement stress. Approximately 2 years ago, Mr. T began to spend increasingly long periods watching the same sports content on television — up to 18 hours per day — and became enraged when interrupted. He has lost interest in grandchildren and friends, with whom he formerly had warm relationships. He has made several sexually inappropriate comments to his wife's sister and a female neighbor, which is completely out of character for a man his wife describes as having had 'strict moral values' throughout their 34-year marriage. He made two unauthorized withdrawals totaling $22,000 from their joint retirement account, the purpose of which he cannot or will not explain. He has urinated in the backyard on multiple occasions and twice inside the house in non-bathroom locations, each time appearing unconcerned about the behavior. He has developed a fixed eating routine, consuming chips and dip at the same time every day, becoming agitated when this is unavailable. His language has become more concrete — he gives one-word answers where he formerly was verbose. His remote alcohol use disorder is well-controlled (12 years sobriety, AA attendance), making active alcoholism unlikely. He is adherent with CPAP and his wife confirms improved sleep quality. The diagnostic challenge in this case includes: (1) prior alcohol use history raising consideration of alcohol-related dementia or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome; (2) vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension) raising vascular dementia; (3) the classic bvFTD behavioral phenotype (disinhibition, hyperorality, stereotypy, loss of empathy) that ultimately favors frontotemporal pathology.

additional_observations: Moderate bifrontal atrophy — more prominent than expected for age and vascular risk factors alone
No mammillary body atrophy or T2 signal change (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome excluded on MRI)
Fazekas 2 periventricular white matter — moderate small vessel disease from hypertension/diabetes
mri.impression: Moderate bilateral frontal atrophy with anterior temporal involvement and relatively preserved posterior cortex. Fazekas grade 2 white matter changes reflect chronic vascular risk factor burden but the degree of frontal atrophy and behavioral syndrome appear disproportionate to the white matter disease alone. No MRI features of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (thalami, mammillary bodies normal). Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.finding: Bilateral frontal hypometabolism — severe. Orbitofrontal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate show 28-34% FDG reduction versus cerebellar reference. This is the most prominent metabolic deficit.
Mild bilateral anterior temporal hypometabolism (12-16% reduction).
PRESERVED — posterior cingulate, parietal association cortex, and occipital lobes show NORMAL FDG uptake. The pattern of posterior preservation with severe frontal reduction is the FTD signature.

Patchy mild hypometabolism in periventricular regions corresponding to Fazekas 2 white matter changes — this secondary vascular effect is present but does NOT account for the severity of frontal hypometabolism.

quantitative_data.vascular_contribution: Minor secondary contribution from Fazekas 2 white matter

output.impression: Severe bilateral frontal hypometabolism with preserved posterior cortex — pattern highly consistent with bvFTD. The FDG-PET frontal changes substantially exceed what would be expected from Fazekas 2 white matter disease alone, confirming primary frontotemporal pathology. The absent posterior cingulate sign excludes Alzheimer's disease.
recommended_actions: Amyloid PET to exclude AD pathology

findings.finding: NEGATIVE — global SUVr 0.89 (below threshold 1.10). No cortical amyloid deposition detected. Frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital regions all below positivity threshold.

output.impression: Negative amyloid PET. Alzheimer's disease pathology excluded. Combined with the FDG-PET frontal predominance pattern and clinical behavioral syndrome, bvFTD diagnosis is confirmed.

findings.finding: Executive function (DKEFS): Severely impaired. Trails switching: 2nd percentile. Color-word inhibition: 1st percentile. Category fluency and letter fluency both impaired.
Social cognition (Faux Pas test): 2/10 scenarios identified correctly (<2nd percentile). Reading the Mind in the Eyes: 14/36 (<2nd percentile) — severe social cognition impairment.

Episodic memory (HVLT-R): Moderate impairment. Delayed recall 3/12 (10th percentile). Recognition 8/12 (25th percentile). HVLT worse than expected for typical bvFTD — may reflect combined frontal-vascular contribution.
Working memory: Digit span forward 5, backward 2 — impaired.
FBI (Frontal Behavioral Inventory, informant): 38/72 — very elevated, indicating severe disinhibition, perseveration, and apathy.

output.impression: Severe executive dysfunction and social cognition impairment consistent with bvFTD. Episodic memory is more impaired than typical bvFTD, likely reflecting a combined frontotemporal and vascular contribution. The behavioral scores (FBI) are severely elevated. Overall profile supports bvFTD as the primary diagnosis.

output.proposed: Symptom management for bvFTD behavioral disturbance: disinhibition, hyperorality, inappropriate behavior
interactions: Lisinopril + sertraline: mild hypotensive effect possible — monitor BP
contraindications: AVOID cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) — not indicated and potentially harmful in FTD
AVOID high-potency antipsychotics with extrapyramidal side effects — FTD patients can develop severe EPS
warnings: Low-dose SSRI (sertraline 50 mg) may reduce disinhibition and stereotyped behavior in bvFTD
Trazodone 100-300 mg may help nighttime agitation and hyperorality
His diabetes management (HbA1c 7.8%) should be simplified given cognitive decline — complex regimens increase error risk
alternatives: Consider simplifying diabetes management with PCP — avoid sulfonylureas (hypoglycemia risk) in cognitively impaired patients

output.query: Wernicke-Korsakoff MRI mammillary body atrophy thiamine bvFTD differential

results.title: MRI findings in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: mammillary body atrophy and thalamic signal change

output.summary: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (WKS) can cause behavioral changes and dementia in alcoholic patients. Key distinguishing features: (1) MRI shows mammillary body atrophy and thalamic T2 signal change (periaqueductal gray involvement in acute phase); (2) thiamine level is low or borderline; (3) behavioral profile is predominantly amnestic (Korsakoff amnesia) rather than the disinhibition/social dysfunction predominant in bvFTD; (4) MoCA typically shows severe memory impairment with relative frontal preservation — opposite of bvFTD profile. In this patient: normal thiamine, normal mammillary bodies, no thalamic signal change, and behavioral profile with severe social dysfunction and disinhibition rather than amnestic predominance — WKS effectively excluded.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia — sporadic — with concurrent small vessel cerebrovascular disease (secondary contributor)

differential.key_feature: Normal thiamine level; normal mammillary bodies on MRI; no thalamic signal change; behavioral profile is disinhibition/social dysfunction rather than amnestic predominance — WKS produces amnestic dementia, not disinhibition syndrome
Fazekas 2 white matter present but FDG-PET frontal hypometabolism substantially exceeds what white matter disease alone would produce; primary FTD pathology with secondary vascular contribution
Amyloid PET negative; no posterior cingulate sign on FDG-PET; behavioral disinhibition/social dysfunction profile more typical of FTD than AD
CPAP-adherent with confirmed improved sleep quality — OSA adequately treated; behavioral changes predate CPAP initiation and progressive despite treatment

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain — frontal atrophy pattern; mammillary body assessment for WKS
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Moderate frontal atrophy; normal mammillary bodies; Fazekas 2 white matter

optimal_actions.action: Thiamine level and standard dementia labs including GGT/MCV for alcohol use assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal thiamine, normal GGT/MCV — WKS and active alcohol use excluded

optimal_actions.action: FDG-PET brain — metabolic pattern; distinguish FTD from vascular dementia
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Severe frontal hypometabolism exceeding vascular white matter contribution; absent posterior cingulate sign

optimal_actions.action: Neuropsychological testing — executive and social cognition profile
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Severely impaired executive function and social cognition; bvFTD profile

critical_actions: Wernicke-Korsakoff must be excluded in any patient with history of alcohol use and behavioral/cognitive syndrome — thiamine level and MRI mammillary body assessment are required
Amyloid PET or CSF Abeta42 must exclude AD before bvFTD diagnosis
Do NOT prescribe cholinesterase inhibitors in FTD
contraindicated_actions: Prescribing oral hypoglycemics with high hypoglycemia risk (sulfonylureas) in cognitively impaired patient — simplify diabetes management
key_reasoning_points: Prior alcohol use history is a red herring — Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is excluded by normal thiamine, normal mammillary bodies on MRI, and a behavioral profile (disinhibition, social dysfunction) rather than the amnestic profile typical of Korsakoff dementia

FDG-PET is essential to distinguish primary FTD from vascular dementia — Fazekas 2 white matter changes can cause cognitive decline but the frontal FDG-PET hypometabolism far exceeds the expected metabolic effect of the white matter disease alone
The diagnostic order matters: MRI first to assess structural pattern and exclude WKS, then FDG-PET for metabolic characterization, then amyloid PET to definitively exclude AD

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute behavioral syndrome to alcohol-related dementia or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: 12 years sobriety with normal thiamine, normal GGT, normal mammillary bodies on MRI, and a disinhibition-predominant (not amnestic) behavioral profile excludes WKS and alcohol-related dementia

red_herrings.data_point: Fazekas grade 2 periventricular white matter changes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose vascular dementia as primary cause
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fazekas 2 cannot explain the severity of behavioral syndrome; FDG-PET shows frontal metabolic changes far exceeding expected vascular white matter contribution — primary FTD with secondary vascular component

metadata.notes: Moderate bvFTD in patient with remote alcohol history and vascular risk factors. Key teaching: thiamine level and mammillary body MRI assessment exclude WKS; FDG-PET severity disproportionate to Fazekas 2 white matter confirms primary FTLD pathology.
